title: The Moon's orbit and its phases

accuracy.evidence: Checked on 24 Nov 2026 against NASA Science 'Moon phases' (the Moon is always half lit; the phase is the share of the sunlit half facing Earth; about 29.5 days new moon to new moon; about 27.3 days per orbit against the stars, which the adult text separates from the phase cycle) and NGSS 5-ESS1-2 and MS-ESS1-1. The lab geometry is true to that model: with sunlight from the left, the Moon goes anticlockwise as seen from above the North Pole, new moon sits on the Sun's side, first quarter a quarter turn on, full moon opposite the Sun; the 'seen from Earth' window draws the lit fraction (1 - cos e)/2 with growing Moons lit on the right, as seen from the Northern Hemisphere, which the adult text states. One day moves the Moon 360/29.5 degrees. The shadow step states eclipses happen only at full moon and are rare because the orbit is tilted.

misconceptions.evidence: Aims at the slips documented by Trundle, Atwood and Christopher (2002) and Baxter (1989): the Moon makes its own light (step 1 prediction, Sun-off button, 'own' slip); Earth's shadow causes phases (step 5 prediction, wrong taps on crescent and half Moons explain the dark part is the Moon's own night side, 'shadow' slip); only the visible part is lit (step 4 prediction about a crescent, every Moon drawn half lit, 'half' slip); full moon placed between Earth and the Sun (step 3 prediction, 'where' slip); the cycle taking a night or a year ('time' slip); shrinking Moons lit on the same side ('side' slip and the order-step refusal).

lab_distinct.evidence: The mechanism belongs to this topic alone: a top-down Sun-Earth-Moon model where the Moon's angle drives both a day counter (360/29.5 degrees per day) and a terminator-drawn 'seen from Earth' window, eight Moons that are all half lit, a shadow band pointing away from the Sun that only the full-moon position can meet, and a phase-ordering task with side-aware refusals. It is not flagmoonph (ages 6-7, which only steps through observed Moon shapes and sorts sky objects); the gate measured under 30% source overlap with every flag_*.js.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each rule is found by acting first: switching the Sun off makes the Moon and the window go dark before the strip says it only reflects light; dragging or stepping days fills the pink orbit track and the day tag reaches 29.5 only after one full trip; dragging the Moon to the far side makes the window full, so the learner sees full moon is opposite the Sun; tapping the crescent Moon shows a half-lit ball in the top view and a thin curve in the window at the same time; tapping crescents in the shadow step is refused because they are off to the side.

predictions.evidence: Four committed predictions, each with a tempting wrong answer the lab then disproves: 'If the Sun switched off, would the Moon still shine?' (yes, it makes its own light); 'Where is the Moon when we see a full moon?' (between Earth and the Sun); 'When we see a thin crescent, how much does the Sun light?' (just the crescent); 'Is a half moon caused by Earth's shadow?' (yes). Tasks cannot complete until a prediction is locked, and the done message names it.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Eight challenge questions; every wrong option carries a tagged slip with its own message: 'own' (no light of its own, Sun-off test), 'shadow' (shadow points away from the Sun, half moon is the night side), 'half' (always half lit, most of it faces away at a crescent), 'where' (new moon between Earth and Sun, full moon opposite), 'time' (about 29.5 days), 'side' (after full moon the lit part shrinks and is on the left), 'shape' (the Moon never changes shape).

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and define each topic word where it first appears (orbit, phase); validate_lessons.py passed the kid and adult readability limits. Lab strips are one to three short lines on a phone, button labels are two or three words, and phase names are given in everyday words (growing crescent, shrinking gibbous) beside the standard names in the adult text.

no_filler.evidence: Each kid paragraph teaches one idea (reflected light; always half lit; the orbit and its length; phases are how much lit half we see, not Earth's shadow). Adult paragraphs give the standards, the precise model including synodic versus sidereal month and the hemisphere caveat, the mistakes, and what the lab does; the content gate found no filler phrases and under 12% overlap with any lesson.

mobile.evidence: Checked on iPhone 13 screenshots in dark and light themes for every step after Show me: the space view and 'seen from Earth' window stack vertically, the orbit radius is sized so the Moon number tags 1 to 8 and the Earth label stay inside the panel, notes are cut to three lines, the seven order cards fit in two rows with readable letters and position badges, and the day buttons and Moon 1 to 8 buttons wrap with nothing clipped.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin (Sun off or on, Look at the Moon, +1 day, +1 week, +3 days, Back 1 day, Moon 1 to 8, Card A to G with aria-labels that describe each shape, such as 'a thin curve lit on the right'). The canvas aria-label updates with every message, challenge feedback is a polite live region, and walk.cjs runs axe WCAG 2.1 AA in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: NASA Science, 'Moon phases' and 'Moon in motion' (science.nasa.gov/moon)
DfE National Curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 5 Earth and space (2013)
Trundle, Atwood and Christopher (2002), Preservice elementary teachers' conceptions of moon phases, Journal of Research in Science Teaching 39(7)
Baxter (1989), Children's understanding of familiar astronomical events, International Journal of Science Education 11(5)
